cells.tense: You are holding the scale steady, and the reading is true enough to act on.
cells.ask: When something lands askew today, adjust the one small thing that is off and say plainly why. Then stop — no second pass.
cells.core:
You're the person holding the scale when feeling runs high. Someone hurts, someone oversteps, and you can name what's fair without tipping the room. What a clean reading gives you: the exchange comes back into proportion, both people stay at the table, and you can close the ledger. That steadiness is the work, and it is going well.

What this balance invites next is smaller than it sounds. Let the fairness you just restored feed the next ordinary thing — a shared meal, a plain decision, an hour that doesn't need weighing — without you standing guard over it. Keep adjusting what's off. Then let the adjusted thing live. The readjustments are the practice; what happens after them is the living.

cells.verb: weighing what is fair in feeling
cells.place: on the floor where balance is restored

cells.tense: You will be checking whether this is fair long after the room has moved on.
cells.ask: At the next decision about what someone owes, leave one thing unsettled for a day — no final verdict. Come back only if it still matters tomorrow.
cells.core:
You're getting ahead of the moment — deciding what's fair before all of it has arrived. Someone is still speaking and the scale is already out, tallying. Once you're braced for the unfairness, every small exchange gets weighed, and the weighing costs more than the thing being weighed. Your read on what you notice is sharp. The rush to close it is what's off.

You can see fairness, and you're using it as a pre-emptive tool instead of a response. When the scale sits right, give and take happen at once, without tally. Leave one charge loose today and let the fair thing find you.

cells.tense: You stopped raising the question of what's fair, and it stopped being asked.
cells.ask: One exchange this week: name the imbalance — one sentence, one person, then drop it. No argument, no fixing.
cells.core:
You can see when something is out of proportion, and you're not saying so. It might not survive the room, or it isn't worth the trouble — either way the scale stays in the drawer. When you don't call the imbalance, what you give and what comes back drift apart, and it gets hard to tell whether fairness is absent or just unspoken. The read is still there.

Fairness flows when the small calibrations happen out loud, not when you wait for them to correct themselves. Borrow from what you already do alone: notice clearly, finish noticing, then return. One exchange, one honest word about the proportions. That's the practice, not a verdict on the person across from you.

cells.tense: The scale is already out and you describe the reading as if the room did the weighing.
cells.ask: Write down one judgment you made this week — the name of it. Next time, say it out loud once. That's the whole move.
cells.core:
You are already reading what's fair in the room — who is off balance, where the exchange runs uneven — and you describe it as the obvious shape of things. Someone else said it first, or the situation made it plain. But the weighing is yours. You do it before anyone speaks, then call it what happened rather than what you judged. Balance is something you can name more simply than you allow yourself.

The recognition is running and your name isn't on it. Try this: name one read you've had as yours — not as the situation's — to one person this week. Not a ruling, just a note about what you noticed. That small acknowledgment is the whole correction; the read itself doesn't have to change.
